tagline: Across the Flint River to Pine Mountain and Roosevelt’s Georgia retreat.
intro: The Meriwether-Pike Scenic Byway makes a 55-mile circuit through Gay, Molena, Manchester and Warm Springs, crossing the Flint River on Flat Shoals Road. Near Manchester, SR 190 follows the Pine Mountain ridge. Georgia DOT designates the corridor a Georgia Scenic Byway and says it celebrates Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s legacy, alongside a covered bridge and the surviving gristmill and pond at Jones Mill.

Journeys to Warm Springs changed with transportation. Nineteenth-century visitors took the railroad to Durand before continuing to the springs; as automobiles spread, tourists went elsewhere and the Meriwether Inn declined. Roosevelt first arrived in 1924 seeking treatment, and built the Little White House in 1932 while governor of New York. Swimming in the spring water brought improvement, though no cure. His experiences in Warm Springs later informed New Deal programs, including the Rural Electrification Administration. The house he built there is now a state historic site, one of the places the byway connects.

Starting the loop at Gay, cross the Flint on Flat Shoals Road and continue southwest to Molena, then toward Manchester. The route returns to Warm Springs via SR 190 before heading north toward Gay. On that northern leg, Red Oak Creek Covered Bridge lies north of Woodbury.

moments.title: Gay
moments.text: The Cotton Fair brings a twice-yearly gathering to Gay: it began in 1972 and takes place each May and October. The fair’s name changed in a rebranding intended to preserve its legacy while avoiding language with painful historical associations. Gay itself counted 110 residents in 2020. The Flint River passes three miles east of town, where the byway crosses it on Flat Shoals Road before turning toward Molena.

moments.title: Little White House
moments.text: Six rooms made of Georgia pine became Roosevelt’s presidential retreat at Warm Springs. Its rooms comprised three bedrooms, an entrance hall, a living room and a kitchen. He built the house in 1932, eight years after first coming to the springs for treatment. On April 12, 1945, while Elizabeth Shoumatoff was painting his portrait, he suffered a cerebral hemorrhage and died. The Unfinished Portrait is displayed in the museum, along with his 1938 Ford convertible equipped with hand controls. The house opened as a museum in 1948; its historic area is now temporarily closed for renovation.
moments.notice: The museum displays the Unfinished Portrait and Roosevelt’s Ford with hand controls.

moments.title: Red Oak Creek Covered Bridge
moments.text: Approximately 2,500 wooden pegs, called trunnels, hold Red Oak Creek Covered Bridge together. Its Town lattice truss crosses the creek north of Woodbury, with long heart-pine sills measuring 15 inches square. Horace King, an enslaved man, probably built it in about 1840. The covered section measures 116 feet, while the full span reaches 412 feet, the longest total span of a covered bridge in Georgia. It entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1973, when it was still in use. Covered Bridge Road, historically called Huel Brown Road, crosses the creek here.

practical: Little White House: The Little White House, servant quarters and guest house are temporarily closed for renovation until further notice. The museum and grounds remain accessible. (checked 2026-10-11)
